summary: Friedrich Carl von Savigny worked in history, archaeology, and other fields. He studied at the universities of Marburg, Jena, and Leipzig, later holding academic posts at Marburg (~1800–1804) and Humboldt University of Berlin (~1810–1842).
Active in history, archaeology, and Indology, he studied at Heidelberg University, Trinity College, Cambridge, and the University of Paris. His teachers included Theodor Goldstücker.

Linguist Friedrich Christian Diez studied at Giessen under Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker and at Göttingen. He spent his academic career at the University of Bonn, holding a post there from ~1823 to 1876.

Working in religious studies, philosophy, and history and archaeology, Friedrich Creuzer studied at the universities of Tübingen and Jena. He held academic posts at Marburg (~1800–1804), Heidelberg (~1804–1845), and Leiden (1809).

A scholar in linguistics, history, and archaeology, Delitzsch studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Jena under Brockhaus, Weber, Fleischer, Dillmann, Curtius, and Schrader. He held professorships at Leipzig (1877), Breslau (1893), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1899).
A Sinologist, Friedrich Ernst August Krause studied at the Seminar für Orientalische Sprachen (~1902–1904). He later held a position at Heidelberg University from ~1923 to 1942.

Linguist Friedrich Ernst Kieckers studied at Bonn, Munich, Berlin, Marburg, and Freiburg, where he was taught by Rudolf Thurneysen. He held posts at Freiburg (1911), Munich (1912, 1917), and the University of Tartu (1921–1938).

Working in history, archaeology, and linguistics, Welcker studied at the University of Giessen (~1801–1803). He subsequently held posts at Giessen (~1809–1816), Göttingen (~1816–1819), and Bonn (~1819–1868).

Friedrich Haag worked in Indology and linguistics, studying at Zurich, Berlin under Albrecht Weber, and Göttingen. He served in secondary schools and held posts at the University of Zurich (1873–1884) and the University of Bern (1887–1914).

Friedrich Heiler, a scholar of religious and Buddhist studies, studied at Munich under Hommel, Dyroff, Kieckers, Kuhn, and Scherman. He held positions at Munich, Greifswald, the Religionskundliche Sammlung, and Marburg (1920–1962).

A Sinologist and historian, Hirth studied at Leipzig, Berlin, Greifswald, and Rostock. He served in the Chinese Maritime Customs Service (1870–1897) and held the Dean Lung Professorship of Chinese at Columbia University (1902–1917).

Working in history, archaeology, and Indology, Friedrich Karl Ginzel was an assistant at the Sternwarte von Oppolzer (1877–1886) and held a post at the Astronomisches Rechen-Institut starting in 1886.

Indologist and linguist Friedrich Karl Slotty studied at Breslau, Greifswald, and Jena under Carl Cappeller and Berthold Delbrück. He taught at the University of Jena, Charles University, and the German University in Prague (1928–1939).

Linguist Friedrich Kluge studied at Leipzig, Freiburg, and Strasbourg under August Leskien, Georg Curtius, and Heinrich Hübschmann. He later held posts at Strasbourg (1880), the University of Jena (1884, 1886), and the University of Freiburg (1893).

Indologist and linguist Friedrich Knauer studied at Tartu, Jena, and Tübingen under Meyer, Delbrück, Cappeller, and Roth. He served as a Privatdozent at Tartu (1884) before becoming a professor at Kyiv University (1886–1914).
Friedrich Kurschat was a linguist who studied at the University of Königsberg from ~1836 to 1840. He subsequently held a post at the University of Königsberg from ~1841 to 1883.

Friedrich Leberecht Wilhelm Schwartz worked in linguistics, religious studies, and other fields. His academic training included studies at the University of Leipzig (~1840–1842) and Humboldt University of Berlin (~1842–1844).
Linguist Friedrich Leo studied at Göttingen and Bonn under Hermann Usener. He held positions at Bonn, Kiel, Rostock, Strasbourg, and the University of Göttingen (1889–1914).
Friedrich Lorentz was a linguist who studied at the University of Leipzig from ~1890 to 1894, completing a Ph.D. under the instruction of Karl Brugmann and August Leskien.

Active in Indology, history, and archaeology, Friedrich Majer studied law at the University of Jena (1791) and was a pupil of Johann Gottfried von Herder. He served as a Privatdozent at Jena (~1801–1802).
